newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Battling Major rows with European leaders.
newsitem.headline: Battling Major rows with European leaders.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, fighting to boost flagging support for his Conservative party ahead of a general election, on Saturday confronted European leaders who have endorsed his rival, Labour leader Tony Blair.

But Major was immediately plunged into a new row over a speech by the European Parliament president, Klaus Haensch, who accused Britain of being out of step with the rest of Europe and of "blackmail tactics" over the mad cow crisis.

Major flew into Dublin for a summit on reforms to the European Union angry that the leaders of Portugal, Austria and the Netherlands had sent videos to last week's Labour party conference backing Blair's bid to become prime minister.

Major believes Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and Portuguese premier Antonio Guterres broke the unwritten rule that a government should not interfere in another state's electoral process, aides said.
An aide to Major said he had spoken personally to the three leaders and all had assured him they intended no personal hurt.
But Major was "hopping mad" about Haensch's speech, which he considered "deeply offensive" and "inappropriate", he said.
Haensch attacked a policy initiated by Major earlier this year to block all EU business until he was given a plan for lifting the worldwide ban on British beef exports.
The EU defused the crisis at its June summit in Florence.
In a speech delivered on Friday night, Haensch warned the rest of Europe would not hold up reform for Britain.
"I fail to see why 14 governments should always have to sacrifice their vision of Europe, and their principles, to keep on board a government which may jump ship in any case.

"If one government is clearly out of step with the 14 others... then the others may have to look at ways of moving forward nonetheless or of postponing final decisions until the government in the minority is prepared to change its position, or until another takes its place," Haensch said.

Major -- angry that another European politician appeared to be endorsing Blair -- complained about the speech to summit host, Irish premier John Bruton, and aides said Britain would be taking it up directly with Haensch.
But the row was the last thing Major needed ahead of next week's Conservative party conference -- the last before the election now no more than seven months away.
The Conservatives, in office for 17 years, are already reeling from a scandal over sleaze involving a former minister.

And Labour has done its best to highlight the conflict within the Conservative party between pro-Europeans and the so-called Eurosceptics opposed to greater European integration and to British entry into a single European currency.
The Austrian and Dutch leaders tried to defuse the row.

Kok said after a morning meeting of socialist summit participants: "That (video) was in my capacity as leader of the Dutch Labour party. So I think he can't be angry with me because I am a social democrat."

Vranitzky, who said Conservative and Socialist leaders in Europe met regularly to swap ideas, added: "If everyone kept feeling insulted just because someone meets somewhere else, there'd be no end to the number of insulted people in Europe."
But Major made little attempt to hide his anger. When asked by a BBC interviewer how he felt about the videos, he replied sharply: "Well they are socialists, aren't they?...
"They would like a socialist government because they think a socialist government would give to Europe those things that a Conservative government never would.
"It is perfectly clear what they are doing... I don't intend to let the sort of socialism that we put aside in the United Kingdom come to the United Kingdom from Europe."
